Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette: At thirty-four, Samir, a single American of Lebanese descent, spent a month fighting for his life when a severe bowel obstruction forced him into emergency surgery and a prolonged ICU stay. He still felt the ghost of that sterile air whenever a new scent crossed his path, and months later, a specific moment in his salon cracked his composure. When a long-time client asked for a quick scalp examination before a trim, that medical procedure acted as a trigger, instantly pulling Samir into a flashback complete with the sharp, antiseptic smell he remembered from the operating theater. That olfactory recall bypassed his mind and settled in his chest, triggering a wave of horror and a sudden spike in his heart rate. His body immediately braced for impact, every muscle locking in preparation for danger, because the trigger had hijacked his nervous system. Waking from a nightmare that same week left him sweating and shaking, and the lingering physiological residue acted as a trigger that carried with it the full physical pain in his lower abdomen, flooding him with fresh fear. What frightened Samir most was not the initial jolt, but what followed. The trigger had convinced him he could no longer trust his body, viewing his racing pulse and trembling hands as proof that his physiology had turned against him. That appraisal did not sit quietly. As he grew convinced that these reactions meant he was losing his grip on reality, the constant tension in his shoulders and jaw tightened further, his nervous system bracing for another collapse. The fear of going crazy became a self-reinforcing loop, amplifying the very symptoms that terrified him. His body felt like an untrustworthy machine, sounding alarms long after he was safe, and that very belief made him hyper-vigilant to potential reminders. He stopped scrolling through client photos on his work phone, knowing that his distrust had turned every image into a minefield that would pull him straight back into the memory of the ward. The salon, once the center of his world, became a space of calculated avoidance. Samir began declining clients who showed signs of fatigue or discomfort, citing "scheduling conflicts" instead of admitting that a routine medical procedure felt like a death sentence. His stylist chair stood empty for weeks, and the steady rhythm of his livelihood frayed into isolation. He spent his days scanning the cutting room floor for anyone who looked unwell, because his appraisal that his body was an enemy forced him to treat every ordinary interaction as a potential threat. When the memory's sudden return made him avoid the very places that sparked it, he simply stopped going to work altogether, leaving his tools gathering dust in a locked drawer. The alertness he carried from the morning would prime the memory to return again, locking him in a cycle he could no longer step out of. Now thirty-eight, Samir walks into therapy carrying the weight of a man who has spent years fighting a war inside his own skin. He seeks help because the avoidance has left him unemployed and financially anxious, but what truly pushes him through the door is the terror that his body will never stop betraying him. He hopes to find a way to quiet the constant alertness and trust himself again, even though he is most afraid that he is already too fractured to ever feel safe in his own head.
